nodes.label: Accusation Audit
nodes.rationale: Preemptively naming the objections Nelson might have (e.g. 'another generic consultancy pitch') strips defensiveness before the meeting turns adversarial and signals a self-awareness that builds fast trust with an analytical, academic profile.

nodes.label: Black Swan (Hidden Leverage)
nodes.rationale: Hypothesis that Nelson's strongest emotional asset is not the CTO title but authorship of the AI security framework itself; a proposal that amplifies visibility and practical validation of his framework — rather than replacing it with a proprietary methodology — wins a far stronger internal sponsor than budget approval alone.

nodes.label: Never Split the Difference — Negotiation Tactics
nodes.norm_label: never split the difference — negotiation tactics
nodes.rationale: Chosen as the negotiation lens for the first conversations with Nelson specifically to avoid a generic consulting approach, given that what is really at stake for him is professional ego, reputational risk as a public cybersecurity figure, and regulatory risk for a bank with 30M+ customers — not price or timeline.

nodes.label: Tactical Empathy (Labeling)
nodes.rationale: Voss technique of labeling the counterpart's likely emotion or concern before they voice it, used here to disarm defensiveness by acknowledging up front that any outside AI proposal must pass through Nelson's own framework.

nodes.label: 'That's Right' vs 'You're Right' Technique
nodes.rationale: The goal is to get Nelson to say 'that's right' (confirming genuine understanding of his position) rather than a superficial 'you're right' that just ends the discussion; achieved by summarizing his view with technical precision before proposing anything new.

nodes.norm_label: aversive stimulus mechanism (security control as aversive stimulus)
nodes.rationale: Nelson's master's thesis (behaviorism / experimental analysis of behavior) empirically showed that a security control acts as an aversive stimulus that reduces the probability of the desired user behavior; this causal mechanism explains why poorly designed AI governance friction suppresses internal adoption and pushes teams toward 'shadow AI' — the core insight an AI transformation pitch should leverage by asking him to apply his own thesis, rather than merely citing the framework.

nodes.label: Calibrated Questions (How/What)
nodes.rationale: Open-ended 'how/what' questions avoid yes/no answers that would let the counterpart shut the conversation down; recommended to probe how the 10-question framework is actually used day-to-day and what still keeps him up at night on AI governance.

nodes.label: Knowledge Item
nodes.rationale: The unit of retrieval: one self-contained technical assertion, typed and tagged, with its own provenance, understandable without opening the original source. Avoid conflating with 'document', 'page', 'record', or 'insight'.

nodes.label: Slack Bot (MCP client)
nodes.rationale: Self-hosted MCP client bundled in this repo so Indicium people can ask questions from Slack; a chat interface only, not a visual dashboard (ADR 0006, ADR 0007).

nodes.label: Dormant ACL filtering model (ADR 0006/0007/0012)
nodes.rationale: ADR table (Section 5) attributes 'filtering logic for an ACL model that Collection ultimately did not build' jointly to ADR 0006, 0007, and 0012 as dormant — but Section 3 of the same document attributes ADR 0006 to 'Slack bot as MCP client' and ADR 0007 to 'self-hosted agent runtime for Slack bot,' which does not reconcile with the ADR table's description of those same numbers. Possible numbering collision or reused ADR IDs in the source document; flagged for review rather than resolved. ADR 0012 has no independent content elsewhere in the document.

nodes.label: ADR 0004: Postgres full-text search before vectors
nodes.norm_label: adr 0004: postgres full-text search before vectors
nodes.rationale: Chose Postgres full-text search before investing in vector search; pgvector extension is provisioned in the dev image but unused — Collection's schema has no tsvector/GIN index yet, and ingestion isn't this repo's to change. Later superseded by ADR 0014 (and text search itself later touched by ADR 0015/0016).

nodes.label: ADR 0006: Slack bot as MCP client in this repo
nodes.norm_label: adr 0006: slack bot as mcp client in this repo

Note: the ADR table in Section 5 also groups ADR 0006 with 0007 and 0012 under 'dormant — filtering logic for an ACL model that Collection ultimately did not build,' a different topic than the Slack-bot rationale given in Section 3. This inconsistency in the source document is flagged for review (see gtc_knowledge_hub_agent_acl_filtering).

nodes.norm_label: adr 0009: text search language config (portuguese to english)
nodes.rationale: Text search language config started as portuguese, then switched to english once Collection made the corpus English-canonical. Later superseded by ADR 0015 (partially superseded by ADR 0014).

nodes.label: ADR 0014: Knowledge Item Contract
nodes.rationale: The load-bearing ADR: formalizes that Collection owns the Knowledge Base schema independently and this repo only reads it (the Retrieval/Collection boundary). Supersedes ADRs 0003, 0004, 0006, 0007, 0008, 0009 (partially), 0010, 0012, and 0013, and amends 0002. Also flags an open governance gap: approval is global, not per-reader, so whether every Indicium person may see a given item's client_name and Engagement Team is an open question with Collection — 'the risk here is inheriting one by silence.' Also states there is no full-text index that could be added, since Collection's schema has no tsvector/GIN and ingestion isn't this repo's to change.

nodes.label: approved_knowledge_item(_expanded) view
nodes.rationale: Read-only view (WHERE status='approved') that enforces the approval quality gate entirely in the data layer — Retrieval application code never filters on status itself, so an unreviewed item cannot leak by accident.

nodes.label: Golden Set
nodes.rationale: A translated, page-level snapshot corpus of real questions mapped to expected Knowledge Items, used to measure whether retrieval quality improves or regresses over time (ADR 0017).

nodes.label: Thin MCP Server (search/get, no synthesis)
nodes.rationale: Exposes only two tools — search and get — over approved Knowledge Items; deliberately has no ask(question) synthesis tool. Rationale: the calling MCP client already has a frontier model better at multi-step retrieval than a pipeline this repo would have to maintain; owning synthesis would mean owning hallucinations, an eval harness, and per-query inference cost for output the client produces anyway (ADR 0001).

nodes.label: ADR 0001: Thin MCP server
nodes.rationale: Deliberately thin server exposing only search/get, no ask(question) tool — the calling MCP client already has a frontier model better at multi-step retrieval; owning synthesis would mean owning hallucinations, an eval harness, and per-query inference cost for output the client produces anyway.

nodes.label: ADR 0017: Golden Set corpus
nodes.rationale: Golden Set corpus is a translated, page-level snapshot used to measure retrieval quality (real questions mapped to expected items) over time.

nodes.label: Open governance gap: approval is global, not per-reader
nodes.norm_label: open governance gap: approval is global, not per-reader
nodes.rationale: Approval is a single global switch; there is no per-role or per-client visibility filter, so whether every Indicium person may see a given approved item's client_name and Engagement Team is, in ADR 0014's own words, 'an open question with Collection... the risk here is inheriting one by silence.' Not yet resolved.

nodes.label: gtc-knowledge-hub-agent
nodes.rationale: MCP server providing the Retrieval half of Indicium's Knowledge Hub: exposes read-only search/get access to approved Knowledge Items so any Technologist can ask what delivery teams have already learned, without knowing where it was written down. Deliberately owns no write path, no answer synthesis, and no per-reader visibility filtering. Maturity is prototype/hackathon-scale — local Docker Postgres only, no managed or production deployment found.

nodes.label: Groundwork (shared vocabulary)
nodes.rationale: Core vocabulary (Knowledge Item, Client, Engagement, Technologist, Engagement Team, Technology, System, Methodology) defined jointly by Retrieval and Collection in CONTEXT.md; neither repo owns it alone.

nodes.label: gtc-knowledge-hub-collector
nodes.rationale: Sibling repository that owns Collection (the /interview skill and load_interview.py) and owns the Knowledge Base Postgres schema independently; this repo (Retrieval) only reads what Collection writes and approves.

nodes.label: ADR 0005: SQLAlchemy behind a repository
nodes.rationale: SQLAlchemy behind a repository pattern so that changes to Collection's underlying schema stay contained to two files, keeping the search/get interface stable even as the schema evolves (also enabled by a pinned, vendored copy of Collection's schema for tests, tests/contract/schema.sql).

nodes.label: ADR 0013: Wiki.js as a source route
nodes.norm_label: adr 0013: wiki.js as a source route
nodes.rationale: Investigated Wiki.js as a source route; found a real permission bug in Wiki.js's GraphQL API and handed it off to Collection, since ingestion isn't this repo's job.

nodes.label: Engagement Team
nodes.rationale: The people who worked on an Engagement, surfaced as 'who might know more.' Explicitly not an access-control list.

nodes.label: Postgres (shared Knowledge Base instance)
nodes.rationale: Shared Postgres instance holding Collection's base tables (knowledge_item, client, engagement, tag, source, interview, redaction_log). Retrieval never reads the base tables directly — only through read-only views.

nodes.label: redaction_log
nodes.rationale: Collection's separate mechanism: records a redaction category (pii, client_identity, commercial, client_financial) and a rationale, but never the removed value itself. This repo never surfaces redaction data.

nodes.label: System
nodes.rationale: Tag dimension for a third-party system integrated with (not chosen), e.g. Tasy, MV. Deliberately never collapsed with Technology, which is what Indicium chose to build with.

nodes.label: success_case (Knowledge Item type)
nodes.rationale: Unlike the other four Knowledge Item types, success_case only ever gets filled in when the interviewer directly asks for it — it is not volunteered or inferred by default.

nodes.label: Per-reader visibility limitation
nodes.rationale: Same gap as the Retrieval side: approval is a single global switch, not scoped by client or role, so there is no per-reader visibility control.

nodes.label: Coverage limitation
nodes.rationale: Interviews are expensive (a multi-hour source read plus a live conversation per person), so most engagement knowledge will simply never get an interview scheduled. There is no passive/background collection mechanism in this repo.

nodes.label: knowledge_item.origin = 'backfill'
nodes.rationale: Exists in the schema for content 'extracted from Source without human validation', but no script in this repo implements it. Used exactly once, to load the original 18-item seed (data/db/seed.sql); the schema comment itself flags it as contradicting ADR 0001 — bootstrap-only, not a steady-state ingestion channel.

nodes.label: Freshness limitation
nodes.rationale: Nothing refreshes on its own — knowledge only updates when someone deliberately re-runs /interview.

nodes.label: Knowledge Bases Component
nodes.rationale: Exposes enterprise data (via vector/graph storage and semantic retrieval) with role-based access control so RAG implementations enforce least-privilege and need-to-know rather than exposing all indexed data to any agent.

nodes.label: Model Access Component
nodes.rationale: Centralizes control over foundation model access with policy enforcement, safety guardrails, and cost tracking/allocation, so model usage stays governable and its spend attributable across the enterprise.

nodes.label: Guardrails (Safety Measures)
nodes.rationale: Bundled into the model access component as a safety measure alongside policy enforcement, so unsafe or out-of-policy model outputs/usages are constrained centrally rather than per-application.

nodes.label: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
nodes.rationale: Applied to enterprise data behind knowledge bases to enforce least-privilege and need-to-know principles, limiting what each agent/actor can retrieve during RAG rather than trusting the model to self-restrict.

nodes.label: Tools Component
nodes.rationale: Provides authorization on top of tool discovery/execution so tools are usable only by the right actors and in the right context, preventing agents from invoking business-critical functions outside their granted scope.

nodes.label: Agentic AI Architecture in the Enterprise
nodes.norm_label: agentic ai architecture in the enterprise
nodes.rationale: Presents a reference architecture organized into layers (applications, agents) and cross-cutting concerns so enterprises can adopt agentic AI while retaining governance, security, and operational control over model access, tools, and data.

nodes.label: Cross-Layer Concerns
nodes.rationale: Observability, security and discoverability are modeled as spanning every layer rather than owned by one layer, so AI operations stay monitored, auditable, and policy-compliant regardless of which component handles a given request.

nodes.label: Accountable and Transparent
nodes.rationale: Modeled as a cross-cutting, vertical characteristic (Fig. 4) rather than a peer characteristic, because transparency and accountability relate to and enable all six other trustworthiness characteristics.

nodes.label: Fair - with Harmful Bias Managed
nodes.source_location: Section 3.7 Fair - with Harmful Bias Managed

nodes.label: Valid and Reliable
nodes.rationale: Positioned as the base/necessary condition for all other trustworthiness characteristics (Fig. 4): an AI system that is not valid and reliable undermines the value of any other characteristic it might possess.

nodes.label: GOVERN Function
nodes.rationale: Designed as a cross-cutting function infused throughout MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE rather than a discrete stage, because governance and compliance considerations must apply continuously across the AI system lifecycle and the organizational hierarchy.

nodes.label: AI RMF Profile
nodes.rationale: The Framework deliberately does not prescribe profile templates, to preserve flexibility for organizations to tailor implementations to their specific sector, use case, risk tolerance, and resources (consistent with the AI RMF being outcome-focused and non-prescriptive, Appendix D).

nodes.label: Risk Tolerance
nodes.rationale: The AI RMF intentionally does not prescribe risk tolerance because acceptable risk levels are highly contextual, shaped by legal/regulatory requirements, sector norms, and organizational priorities that vary across users.

nodes.label: Attributes of the AI RMF
nodes.rationale: Ten design attributes established at the outset of Framework development and used to guide its development: risk-based/resource-efficient/pro-innovation/voluntary; consensus-driven; plain-language yet technically sufficient; common taxonomy/terminology; easily usable and compatible with other risk management; broadly applicable across sectors and technologies; outcome-focused and non-prescriptive; standards-aware; law- and regulation-agnostic; and a living document. Together they explain why the AI RMF favors flexibility and voluntary adoption over prescriptive mandates.

nodes.label: Shadow AI
nodes.rationale: Uso de ferramenta, extensão ou API não aprovada que remove a visibilidade de TI sobre o dado corporativo. Já há usuários do C6 'estourando' o volume de tokens esperado — motiva a frente Knowledge Workers a levar IA generativa governada às áreas de negócio para reduzir esse risco.

nodes.label: Os Três Não Negociáveis
nodes.rationale: Nada do C6 sai do ambiente do C6; nenhuma IA sem autorização; na dúvida, DM. Justificado pela política de DLP do cliente: qualquer informação confidencial de um banco precisa ficar dentro da rede do banco — não é burocracia, é regra formal do cliente (reforçado por Tadashi na call em resposta à pergunta de Gabriel Bernardo sobre ferramentas de transcrição externas).

nodes.label: Esteira AI-nativa (redesenho do SDLC)
nodes.rationale: Objetivo principal do patrocinador Paulo Pituba/Thiago Ribeiro, segundo Igor Benincá: o C6 gasta hoje ~R$10-15 milhões/ano com consultorias terceiras de desenvolvimento e espera eliminar esse custo redesenhando o SDLC com Kiro. Esse número é achado exclusivo da transcrição, não aparece no deck nem no manual de bordo.
